items.prompt: In which direction is Arabic text written?
rubric: Arabic script runs from right to left.
Left to right is the direction of English and other Latin-script languages.

items.prompt: How many letters does the standard Arabic alphabet have?
rubric: The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters.
22 is the Hebrew count and 26 is the English count.

items.prompt: Which element is the Arabic definite article, meaning 'the'?
rubric: ال (al-) is attached to the front of a noun to mean 'the'.
The other options mean 'in', 'this' and 'and'.

items.prompt: What does the Arabic word شكرًا (shukran) mean?
rubric: شكرًا means 'thank you'.
Learners often confuse set phrases such as 'please' and 'sorry' with it.

items.prompt: Which set names the three short vowel marks of Arabic?
rubric: The short vowel marks are fatha (a), damma (u) and kasra (i).
Alif, waw and ya are long vowel letters, and the other sets are different marks.

items.prompt: Which letters are used to write the long vowels ā, ū and ī? Select all that apply.
rubric: Alif, waw and ya carry the long vowels ā, ū and ī.
Ba and ra are ordinary consonants.

items.prompt: You meet your Arabic teacher at 8 a.m. and want to greet her with the standard Modern Standard Arabic phrase for 'Good morning'. You try to recall the phrase you learned in class. Which phrase is it?
rubric: صباح الخير is 'Good morning'.
مساء الخير is the evening greeting, تصبح على خير is 'good night' and مع السلامة is 'goodbye'.

items.prompt: Why does the letter ع look different at the start of a word than at the end of a word?

options.label: Its shape marks whether the word is definite or indefinite
Its sound changes with the gender and number of the word
The initial form marks a noun and the final form marks a verb
Most letters take different forms depending on their position and joining

rubric: Most Arabic letters have separate, initial, medial and final forms depending on how they join.
The shape of a letter does not signal grammar or sound change.

items.prompt: Which of these words is normally classified as feminine?
rubric: Words ending in tā' marbūṭa (ة) are usually feminine.
The other nouns are masculine and have no such ending.

items.prompt: How does Modern Standard Arabic usually express 'The boy is big' (الولد كبير) in the present tense?

options.label: It always places the pronoun هو between the noun and adjective
It uses no verb for 'is'; the noun and adjective stand side by side
It always inserts the verb كان before the adjective
It attaches a special ending to the adjective meaning 'is'

rubric: Present-tense nominal sentences have no verb 'to be'.
Learners transfer the English need for a copula and add كان or a pronoun.

items.prompt: The phrase الشمس 'the sun' is pronounced ash-shams, not al-shams. What explains this?

options.label: The word is feminine, so ال changes its vowel to a
The lam of ال merges into the following sun letter, which is doubled
The letter ش is silent when it follows the definite article
Stress on the first syllable replaces the lam with a sh sound

rubric: Before sun letters, the lam of ال assimilates and the next letter is doubled.
Gender and stress do not cause this change.

items.prompt: What does the ending ـان in طالبان (ṭālibān) indicate?
rubric: The ending ـان marks the dual, meaning exactly two.
Arabic has singular, dual and plural, which learners may overlook.

items.prompt: Which statements about the Arabic script are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: Letters like ا, د and ر do not join to the following letter
Each letter has one fixed shape wherever it appears
Short vowels are usually left unwritten in everyday texts
Capital letters mark the start of names and sentences
Most letters join to the letters next to them within a word

rubric: Everyday texts omit short vowels, most letters join, and a few letters such as ا, د and ر do not join forward.
Arabic has no capital letters and letters change shape by position.

items.prompt: In a newspaper you see the word كتب written with no vowel marks. A friend says native readers still read it without trouble. You wonder how they decide between readings such as kataba 'he wrote' and kutub 'books'. What best explains this?

options.label: The first letter always shows which vowels the word has
Readers use the sentence context and known word patterns to supply the vowels
A hidden dot above each letter tells readers which vowel to say
Readers guess randomly, since all readings are equally correct

rubric: Fluent readers infer vowels from context, grammar and word patterns.
The script does not mark vowels through letters or dots in everyday text.

items.prompt: In which word is the definite article ال pronounced by assimilating its lam to the first letter of the noun (a 'sun letter' case)?
rubric: ش is a sun letter, so the lam assimilates and the word is said ash-shams.
Distractors begin with moon letters (ق, ك, ب), where the lam is pronounced.

items.prompt: A noun such as مدرسة (madrasa) ends in ة (ta marbuta). What does this ending most often signal?

options.label: The noun is a past tense verb
The noun is a plural noun
The noun is a feminine singular noun

rubric: Ta marbuta typically marks feminine singular nouns.
Learners confuse it with plural endings or with definiteness, which is shown by ال.

items.prompt: In كتاب كبير 'a big book' and مدرسة كبيرة 'a big school', why does the adjective gain ة in the second phrase?

options.label: It becomes plural to match the noun's number
It marks the phrase as definite, like English 'the'
It agrees with the noun, which is feminine
It shows the adjective comes before the noun

rubric: Arabic adjectives agree with their noun in gender, so a feminine noun takes a feminine adjective.
Distractors mix up gender agreement with number, definiteness or word order.

items.prompt: Why does الولد طالب ('The boy is a student') contain no word for 'is'?

options.label: The verb 'is' is written only when the subject is plural
Only questions need a written verb meaning 'is'
The word طالب already contains a hidden verb meaning 'is'
Present-tense sentences of this kind need no verb 'to be'

rubric: MSA nominal sentences link subject and predicate without a present-tense copula.
Distractors invent hidden verbs or plural/question rules that do not exist.

items.prompt: Which letter does NOT connect to the letter that follows it when writing a word in Arabic script?
rubric: د is one of the non-connecting letters (with ا, ذ, ر, ز, و).
ب, ن and س connect on both sides.

items.prompt: Which of these marks represent short vowels in Arabic? Select all that apply.
rubric: Fatha, damma and kasra are the three short vowels (a, u, i).
Sukun marks the absence of a vowel, so it is not a vowel.

items.prompt: A learner sees the unvowelled word كتب in a newspaper headline and asks how readers know whether it means 'wrote' or 'books'. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Short vowels are usually unwritten, so context and grammar decide
Newspapers add a hidden sukun that always marks verbs
Only the dots on the first letter fix which reading is meant
The shape of the final letter shows whether it is a verb or noun

rubric: Everyday MSA texts omit short vowels; readers rely on context and grammar.
Distractors invent letter-shape or hidden-mark rules.

items.prompt: Which phrase correctly means 'the big house' (بيت is masculine)?
rubric: Both noun and adjective take ال in a definite noun phrase.
البيت كبير is a full sentence, 'The house is big'.

items.prompt: Which form means 'her book'?
rubric: The suffix ـها means 'her'.
ـي is 'my', ـه is 'his', ـك is 'your'.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly asks 'Where is the school?'
rubric: أين means 'where'.
متى is 'when', كيف is 'how', ماذا is 'what'.

items.prompt: The root د-ر-س relates to studying. Using the pattern that gives مكتبة (library) from ك-ت-ب, which word means 'school', a place of study?
rubric: The place pattern مَفْعَلة gives مدرسة from د-ر-س.
Other options are different derived forms: a student, a lesson, studied.

items.prompt: The past verb كتب means 'he wrote'. Which form means 'I wrote'?
rubric: The ending ـتُ marks first person singular 'I'.
ـتَ is 'you (m.)', ـنا is 'we', ـتْ is 'she'.

items.prompt: Which phrases show correct noun-adjective gender agreement? Select all that apply.
rubric: Feminine nouns need feminine adjectives ending in ة.
بنت صغير pairs a feminine noun with a masculine adjective.

items.prompt: You are in a café in Amman and want to politely order one coffee for yourself. Which sentence should you say?
rubric: أريد means 'I want' and من فضلك means 'please', so the order is polite and correct.
Other options use 'you want', 'I am coffee' or 'he wants', which change the meaning.

items.prompt: How do you say "the teacher's (f.) book" as a correct idafa (construct) phrase in MSA?
rubric: In an idafa the first term has no ال and the second term is definite and in the genitive: كتاب المعلمة.
Putting ال on the first term (الكتاب المعلمة) is the common mistake; كتاب معلمة means 'a teacher's book'.

items.prompt: Which sentence correctly says "I did not write the letter" (simple past negation)?
rubric: لم plus a jussive present-tense verb negates the past: لم أكتب.
لن negates the future, and لا or ما plus the present does not give a past meaning.

items.prompt: Which is the correct way to write "three books" (كتاب is masculine)?
rubric: Numbers 3 to 10 take the opposite gender of the noun (masculine noun gets ثلاثة) and a genitive plural noun: ثلاثة كتب.
ثلاث is for feminine nouns, and a singular noun after the number is incorrect.

items.prompt: Which is the correct noun phrase for "the big houses" (the noun is a non-human plural)?
rubric: A non-human plural takes a feminine singular adjective that matches in definiteness: البيوت الكبيرة.
البيوت كبيرة is a complete sentence ('the houses are big'), not a noun phrase.

items.prompt: Apply the sun-letter rule: how is the definite article pronounced in الطالب ("the student")?

options.label: aṭ-ṭālib, with the lam assimilated to ṭ
a-ṭālib, with the lam dropped entirely

rubric: ط is a sun letter, so the lam of ال assimilates to it and the letter is doubled: aṭ-ṭālib.
Pronouncing the lam is the moon-letter pattern, as in القمر.

items.prompt: Which of these are correct nominative dual forms? Select all that apply.
rubric: The nominative dual ends in ـان: معلمان, طالبتان, بابان.
كتابين is the accusative/genitive dual, and معلمون is a sound masculine plural, not a dual.

items.prompt: Sara is writing a diary entry in MSA about her friend Layla. She wants to say "Layla went to school yesterday." She knows the verb root ذ-ه-ب and that the past tense is built with suffixes. Which sentence should she write?
rubric: A past verb before a feminine subject takes the feminine suffix ـت: ذهبت ليلى.
ذهب is masculine, تذهب is present, and ستذهب is future, so none fits 'went yesterday'.

items.prompt: A learner writes: الطالباتُ يدرسون في الجامعة. Which analysis of the error is correct?

options.label: The verb يدرسون is masculine plural, but a feminine plural subject needs يدرسن
The preposition في must be replaced because الجامعة is a feminine noun
The verb must come before the subject, so the sentence needs reordering
The subject الطالبات must be indefinite when it begins a sentence

rubric: In a nominal sentence the verb agrees fully with the subject, so a feminine plural subject needs يدرسن.
Word order is not the problem: a nominal sentence with the subject first is valid.

items.prompt: Why is ذهب الطلاب considered more standard than ذهبوا الطلاب for "the students went"?

options.label: A verb before its plural subject normally stays singular, agreeing only in gender
A verb before its subject must take the plural ending to show the number
The definite subject الطلاب requires a dual verb form in this position
Past verbs never take the plural ending in any verbal sentence structure

rubric: When the verb precedes its subject, it agrees in gender but stays singular.
The plural ending ـوا appears when the subject is a pronoun or comes first, which is why the plural-verb distractor is tempting.

items.prompt: Which word does NOT derive from the root ع-ل-م (knowledge)?
rubric: علاج (treatment) comes from the root ع-ل-ج.
The other words share ع-ل-م and its meaning of knowing or teaching; similar spelling misleads learners.

items.prompt: A learner negates "The student is in the house" as لم الطالب في البيت. What is the main problem?

options.label: الطالب must be indefinite after any negative particle
في must become على after a negative particle in MSA
لم can only negate future time, so لن would be needed
لم needs a jussive verb right after it; a nominal sentence needs ليس

rubric: لم is followed directly by a jussive verb; a present nominal sentence is negated with ليس: ليس الطالب في البيت.
لم refers to the past, not the future, so the claim about the future is wrong.

items.prompt: Compare البيت الكبير and البيت كبير. Why is only the second a complete sentence?

options.label: The first lacks a verb, and every Arabic sentence needs a verb
In the first, both words are definite, so الكبير cannot be a predicate
In the first, the adjective matches the noun's definiteness, forming a phrase; an indefinite predicate makes a sentence
The second has a feminine ending, which marks a full statement

rubric: A definite adjective after a definite noun is a modifier ('the big house'); an indefinite predicate gives 'the house is big'.
Arabic nominal sentences need no verb, so the first distractor is wrong.

items.prompt: A learner writes: هذا البنات يلعبون في الحديقة الجميل. Which errors does the sentence contain? Select all that apply.

options.label: يلعبون should be the feminine plural يلعبن
هذا does not agree with البنات (هؤلاء is needed)
في should be replaced by على
الجميل should be feminine to agree with الحديقة
البنات should be indefinite after هذا

rubric: The demonstrative, the verb and the adjective all fail to agree in gender or number with their nouns.
في is correct for 'in the garden', and a demonstrative before a definite noun is standard.

items.prompt: A learner writes: قرأتُ الكتابُ الجديدُ. Her tutor says the case endings are wrong, though the word order is fine. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: The adjective only should be accusative, since nouns keep nominative endings
The verb should be passive, so the nominative endings would then be correct
The adjective should be indefinite, because adjectives never copy a noun's definiteness
The book is the object of قرأتُ, so noun and adjective should both be accusative: الكتابَ الجديدَ

rubric: The object of an active verb is accusative, and the adjective copies the noun's case: الكتابَ الجديدَ.
Adjectives agree with their noun in case and definiteness, so partial or indefinite fixes are wrong.

items.prompt: Which vowelled phrase means 'the book of the new student' (the student is the new one)?
rubric: The adjective copies the case of the noun it modifies; الطالبِ is genitive, so الجديدِ is genitive too.
الجديدُ is nominative and modifies كتابُ ('the student's new book'); the others break idafa rules (no tanwin or article on the first term).

items.prompt: A learner writes `البيتُ كبيرٌ` intending the phrase 'the big house'. Why does this not mean that?

options.label: The adjective is in the wrong gender for the noun, so it cannot modify it and is read as a new sentence.
The adjective must precede the noun in a phrase, so this order turns the phrase into a sentence about size.
The adjective has no article, so it is read as a predicate and the words form the sentence 'the house is big'.
The noun needs tanwin to be modified by an adjective, so without it the two words form a separate clause.

rubric: An adjective modifying a definite noun must also be definite; an indefinite adjective after a definite noun is a predicate.
Distractors invent word-order, tanwin or gender rules that do not govern this contrast.

items.prompt: Three of these words share the place-noun pattern مَفْعَل ('place of doing'). Which one does not?
rubric: مِفْتاح follows the instrument pattern مِفْعال from the root ف ت ح.
The other three are place nouns from the roots ط ب خ, ل ع ب and ك ت ب.

items.prompt: A learner writes `إنَّ المعلمونَ مجتهدونَ`. What is the faulty step?

options.label: إنَّ should be replaced by كانَ, because a nominal sentence needs a verb to govern the case of its words.
المعلمونَ should be accusative, المعلمينَ, because it is the subject noun that إنَّ puts in the accusative.
المعلمونَ should be genitive, المعلمينَ, because إنَّ acts like a preposition and governs the noun after it.
مجتهدونَ should be accusative, مجتهدينَ, because the predicate of إنَّ is accusative along with its subject.

rubric: إنَّ puts its subject in the accusative while the predicate stays nominative, so only the first word is wrong.
The strongest distractor wrongly accusativises the predicate; that is the kāna pattern, not inna.

items.prompt: For numerals 3 to 10 the numeral takes the opposite gender form to the counted noun. Which phrase breaks this rule?
rubric: كتب is the plural of the masculine كتاب, so the numeral needs the form with taa marbuta: خمسةُ كتبٍ.
Learners are misled by the plural looking 'feminine' or by the broken plural pattern.

items.prompt: Consider `كانَ الطقسُ جميلاً` and `إنَّ الطقسَ جميلٌ`. Which statements correctly analyse the case endings? Select all that apply.

options.label: In the second sentence, جميلٌ is nominative because إنَّ leaves both of its words nominative.
In the first sentence, جميلاً is accusative because it is the predicate (khabar) of كانَ.
In the first sentence, جميلاً is accusative because any adjective after a definite noun is accusative.
In the first sentence, الطقسُ is nominative because it is the subject (ism) of كانَ.
In the second sentence, the subject takes the accusative and the predicate stays nominative, the reverse of كانَ.

rubric: كانَ keeps its subject nominative and puts its predicate in the accusative; إنَّ does the opposite.
The distractors invent a general adjective rule or claim إنَّ changes nothing.

items.prompt: A learner translating 'I saw two female teachers in the library' writes `رأيتُ معلمتانِ في المكتبةِ`. Her tutor circles the dual noun. She has used the correct stem and the correct dual marker for a feminine noun. What is the problem?

options.label: The dual is the object of the verb, so it takes the accusative ending: معلمتينِ.
The dual of a feminine noun is built on the masculine pattern, so the form should be معلمانِ.
The dual loses its final nūn here because a prepositional phrase follows it, giving معلمتا.
The dual must agree with the verb, so the verb should become the dual form رأيتما.

rubric: The dual marks case with ـانِ in the nominative and ـيْنِ in the accusative and genitive; an object is accusative.
Distractors confuse dual endings with verb agreement, the idafa nūn drop, or gender patterns.

items.prompt: You must look up `استخراج` in a root-ordered dictionary. Criterion: the fewest wasted lookups. Which strategy is best?

options.label: Look under the first letter ا and scan the entries for the word spelled exactly as it is written in the text.
Look under ت, the first letter after the initial hamza, since that letter begins the stem of the word.
Strip the prefix and pattern letters to reach the root خ ر ج, then look under that root.
Look under س, because the prefix است marks the derived form and the dictionary groups words by prefix.

rubric: Root-ordered dictionaries list derived forms under the root, so removing the form VIII-type pattern letters is the efficient route.
Distractors treat the dictionary as alphabetical by surface spelling or by prefix.

items.prompt: You prepare a reading text for intermediate learners. Criteria: train reading from context as in real newspapers, yet prevent misreading of words that context cannot settle. Which diacritics policy fits best?

options.label: Leave the text unvowelled except on ambiguous words, where a short vowel or shadda is added.
Remove all diacritics, even from ambiguous words, to match the look of authentic newspapers exactly.
Vowel only the final case endings, because the internal vowels can always be guessed from the root.
Fully vowel every word so that no learner ever has to guess a word form or a case ending.

rubric: Selective vowelling keeps context-reading practice while resolving genuine ambiguity.
Full vowelling removes the training; no vowelling risks misreads; ending-only vowelling ignores internal ambiguity.

items.prompt: You email a professor you have never met to request an appointment. Criteria: formal register, respectful tone, standard MSA. Which opening and request is best?

options.label: أهلاً يا أستاذ، أنا عايز أقابلك بكرة لو سمحت
مرحباً يا صديقي، متى تكون فاضياً هذا الأسبوع؟
السلام عليك أيها الأستاذ، حدد لي موعداً للقاء اليوم
حضرة الأستاذ الفاضل، تحية طيبة وبعد، أرجو التكرم بتحديد موعد للقاء

rubric: Honorific address, a standard greeting formula and a polite request verb meet all the criteria.
Distractors use dialect, over-familiar address, or a blunt imperative.

items.prompt: A learner says that dropping the final vowel of the last word in a sentence when reading aloud is 'sloppy', since every case ending must always be pronounced. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Right: the case ending is part of the word and must always be pronounced, or the grammatical meaning is lost.
Wrong: case endings are used only in poetry and recitation, never in formal speech or news reading.
Wrong: at a pause the final short vowel is normally dropped, so leaving it off at sentence end is standard.
Right in speech but wrong in writing, where pausal forms are required for every sentence-final word.

rubric: Pausal form (waqf) drops final short vowels, so the learner's rule is over-strict.
Distractors overstate the rule or wrongly claim case endings are absent from formal speech.

items.prompt: A learner has six months and wants to read news headlines reliably. Criteria: reading speed on news texts and dependable parsing of unfamiliar words. Which plan is best?

options.label: Memorise 3,000 isolated words from an alphabetical list first, and begin reading only after finishing the entire list.
Learn the root-and-pattern system plus high-frequency news vocabulary, and read headlines daily with partial vowels.
Study a spoken dialect first, assuming news Arabic can be guessed once speech is understood and basic words are known.
Master every case ending in fully vowelled grammar tables before reading any authentic text, to avoid fossilised errors.

rubric: Roots and patterns let a reader parse unseen words, and daily headline practice builds speed.
The distractors delay authentic reading or rely on a different variety.

items.prompt: A learner states the rule: 'An adjective copies its noun's gender and number.' Which judgments about this rule are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is incomplete: the adjective must also match the noun's definiteness and case.
It overgeneralises: a non-human plural noun normally takes a feminine singular adjective.
It holds for human plural nouns, as in طلابٌ جددٌ.
It is fully accurate and needs no additions.
It fails for dual nouns, which always take a singular adjective.

rubric: Agreement also covers definiteness and case, and non-human plurals take feminine singular adjectives.
Duals take dual adjectives, so the claim that they fail is wrong.

items.prompt: A translator renders 'He said that he is tired' for a formal news bulletin. The reviewer's criteria: follow MSA conventions for reporting speech after قال, and keep correct case endings. Four drafts are submitted. Which is best?
rubric: After قال, the reported statement opens with إنَّ, and its predicate stays nominative.
Distractors use أنَّ, a non-standard أنْ هو, or put the predicate of إنَّ in the accusative.

items.prompt: A writer wants the vocalized phrase to mean 'the student's book, which is new' (the BOOK is new, not the student). Judged against that meaning and correct case, which vocalization is best?
rubric: The adjective must agree in case with كتاب (nominative), so الجديدُ marks the book as new.
الجديدِ would agree with الطالبِ and mean 'the new student'; the other options break case rules.

items.prompt: A learner must write 'He did not say anything' in formal MSA using لم. Judged against the rule for jussive forms of hollow verbs, which form is correct?
rubric: In the jussive of a hollow verb, the long vowel shortens before the sukun, giving يَقُلْ.
Distractors keep the long vowel or use the wrong mood ending.

items.prompt: A news editor needs verb-first order in formal MSA for 'The students attended.' Judged against standard agreement rules, which sentence is correct?
rubric: A verb preceding its plural subject stays singular in MSA.
حضروا الطلاب is the common error of pluralising a verb that comes first.

items.prompt: Judged against the rule of reversed gender agreement for numerals 3 to 10, which is the correct phrase for 'three female students'?
rubric: Numerals 3 to 10 take the opposite gender of the counted noun, so the feminine noun takes ثلاثُ without ta marbuta, followed by a genitive plural.
ثلاثةُ matches gender and ignores the reversal; the others also break noun number or case.

items.prompt: A publisher prints texts for adult intermediate readers. Criteria: keep pages readable, and prevent misreading of minimal pairs such as كَتَبَ/كُتُب. Which vocalization policy best meets both?

options.label: Mark short vowels only on words whose reading is ambiguous in context, leaving the rest bare
Mark only the final letter of each word, since case endings cause most misreadings
Mark every short vowel and case ending on every word, so no reading is left to guess
Remove all marks, since context always resolves every ambiguity for adult readers

rubric: Selective vocalization balances readability with disambiguation.
Full marking clutters the page, no marks ignores real ambiguity, and final-letter-only misses root-vowel ambiguities.

items.prompt: A teacher evaluates claims about the idafa (genitive construction) as in كتابُ الطالبِ. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.label: The second term is always nominative whatever the sentence role.
The definiteness of the whole phrase comes from the second term.
An adjective of the first term follows the whole phrase and agrees with the first term's case.
The first term takes ال whenever the second term is definite.
The first term drops tanween and the definite article.

rubric: The first term is bare, the second term gives definiteness, and the adjective of the first term goes after the second term.
The second term is genitive, and ال on the first term is wrong.

items.prompt: An editor reviews a wire translation of 'He said that the meeting was postponed.' The house style is formal MSA, and the reported clause must begin right after the verb of speaking. Which version is best?
rubric: After قال, a reported clause opens with إنّ (kasra), and its subject is accusative.
أنّ is the common error after قال; إنْ is conditional and لأنّ means 'because'.

items.prompt: Construct 'The teacher is not a liar' using ليس, with the predicate in the accusative and no added preposition. Which sentence meets both constraints?
rubric: ليس behaves like كان: the subject is nominative and the predicate is accusative.
بكاذبٍ adds the preposition, and the others have the wrong case or particle.

items.prompt: Select the form that builds the Form X verbal noun (pattern istif'aal) from the root ع-م-ل, giving the meaning 'use'.
rubric: Form X masdar follows استفعال, giving استعمال.
مستعمِل is the participle, تعامل is Form VI, and إعمال is Form IV.

items.prompt: Select the spelling of 'questions' (plural of سؤال) that satisfies the standard hamza-seat rule, where the strongest vowel decides the seat.
rubric: The hamza follows a fatha and carries a kasra, and kasra is stronger, so the seat is a ya without dots.
Other options use the wrong seat or drop the initial hamza.

items.prompt: Construct 'No student came except Ali.' The sentence must use the preferred construction after a negated clause with a general noun, where the excepted noun matches the case of 'student'. Which sentence works?
rubric: After a negative with a general noun, the excepted noun is a substitute that takes the same case, here nominative.
Accusative is the form for positive clauses, and the genitive is simply wrong.

items.prompt: Build 'the two teachers of the school' as the subject of a sentence, as an idafa in the nominative. Which phrase meets the rules for a dual first term?
rubric: A dual first term drops its nun and has no ال, with nominative ـا.
The other options keep the nun, keep ال, or use the oblique ending.

items.prompt: Compose 'If you study, you will succeed' as a possible (real) condition in formal MSA using إنْ. Which constructions satisfy this? Select all that apply.
rubric: After إنْ, both verbs are jussive if present, or past tense with future sense.
Indicative endings are wrong after إنْ, and لو expresses an unreal condition.

items.prompt: A textbook designer wants one pronunciation rule that predicts, without a memorised list, when the lam of ال assimilates to the next consonant (sun letters). Which rule best fits all fourteen sun letters?

options.label: Assimilate before consonants made with the tongue tip or blade at the teeth or ridge
Assimilate before emphatic consonants made with the back of the tongue raised
Assimilate before consonants made deep in the throat, far from the lam's position
Assimilate before consonants whose written shape has a dot above or below

rubric: Sun letters are the coronal consonants, produced near the lam's own place of articulation.
The others confuse the rule with throat sounds, dots in the script, or emphasis alone.
